content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published a guideline in 2022 on the control and elimination of human schistosomiasis. This guideline is available in both electronic and print versions, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-004160-8 and 978-92-4-004161-5. The original English version remains the authoritative edition. The guideline includes recommendations on the safety of praziquantel for treating schistosomiasis, verification of transmission interruption, and strategies for dissemination, implementation, and evaluation. It also outlines future research needs and provides references and annexes. These annexes include lists of contributors, declarations of interest, evidence quality assessments (GRADE), PICO questions, and classifications of infection intensity. The guideline was developed with contributions from a diverse group of experts, chaired by Paul Hagan from the University of Hull, UK, and co-chaired by M. Hassan Murad from the Mayo Clinic, USA. The systematic review team and external reviewers also provided critical input. The guideline development process was coordinated by Amadou Garba Djirmay under the leadership of Mwelecele Malecela, Director of the WHO Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases. Financial support for the guideline was provided by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. Key terms used in the guideline are defined as follows: 1. Control: Reduction of disease incidence, prevalence, morbidity, and/or mortality to a locally acceptable level through public health efforts, requiring continued interventions to maintain the reduction. 2. Elimination as a public health problem: Achieving measurable public health targets set by WHO for a specific disease, requiring ongoing actions to maintain targets and prevent reintroduction. 3. Interruption of transmission: No new human cases of infection in a defined area, with minimal risk of reintroduction, achieved through deliberate efforts. Verification is required to document this achievement. 4. Haematuria: Presence of red blood cells in urine, visible as red or brown discoloration (macrohaematuria) or detectable only with reagent strips (microhaematuria). 5. High-prevalence settings: Areas where schistosomiasis prevalence among school-aged children is ≥50% by parasitological methods or ≥75% by point-of-care urine assays. 6. Intensity of infection: The number of schistosomes infecting an individual, measured indirectly by counting eggs in feces (eggs per gram) or urine (eggs per 10 mL). WHO classifies infections as light, moderate, or heavy based on egg counts. 7. Low-prevalence settings: Areas where schistosomiasis prevalence among school-aged children is <10% by parasitological methods or <30% by point-of-care assays. 8. Mass drug administration (MDA): Distribution of medicines to an entire population in a given area, regardless of symptoms or infection status, with possible exclusion criteria. 9. Moderate-prevalence settings: Areas where schistosomiasis prevalence among school-aged children is ≥10% and <50% by parasitological methods or ≥30% and <75% by point-of-care assays. 10. Morbidity: The impact of schistosomiasis on health and well-being, which may include overt symptoms (e.g., blood in urine, anemia, genital lesions, chronic pain) or subtle effects (e.g., intestinal damage, liver pathology, stunted growth, impaired cognitive development). 11. Persistent hot spots: Communities with ≥10% prevalence of Schistosoma spp. infection that fail to respond adequately to two annual rounds of preventive chemotherapy, despite ≥75% treatment coverage. An inadequate response is provisionally defined as less than a one-third reduction in prevalence compared to baseline surveys. The guideline emphasizes the importance of evidence-based approaches and collaboration among experts to achieve the control and elimination of schistosomiasis.
